entries.answer: Buhaton means to do or to make, and it is the ordinary verb for any action whose object is a thing rather than a person. It is used in three tenses that matter: buhaton for the past or completed, magbuhaton for the ongoing or future, and buhatona for the command or request. The big trap is that it is not the general verb for everything, and the difference is a matter of what is being acted on: saying buhaton og sulat covers writing a letter, but it is not how you ask someone to eat, go or sleep, since those use their own verbs. Another trap is the accent. Dili kaayo, meaning it is not good, uses the same word as kaayo meaning good, and beginners regularly drop the y and turn one into the other.

entries.answer: Kaon means to eat, and in Cebuano it is the word for both eating and drinking, which is a detail that trips up people coming from English where those are separate verbs. The root is kaon with a prefix that carries the tense, so nakaon for ate, magkaon for eating or will eat, and kaona for the food itself. There is a related verb, inom, for drinking, but in practice kaon covers both unless you are being specific. The polite form adds a prefix, so kaon ka means please eat, and the way it is said to a guest is close to an instruction rather than an offer. The opposite is not a single word but a construction using dili, since saying dili kaon means not eat as an instruction while unya ka kaon means I have already eaten.

entries.answer: Sulat means both to write and the thing written, a letter or a document, and one word carries the action and the result, which is common in Filipino and Bisaya. Its tenses follow the pattern: nagsulat for wrote, nagsulat for is writing depending on whether the subject is emphasised, and sulata for the written message itself. A separate and important sense is text as a message on a phone, since that usage is now the more common one in everyday conversation. The noun also means ink or pen in some contexts, so sulat is both the instrument and what it produces. The verb for describing a picture or diagram is another word entirely, hain, and confusing the two is the usual error when a speaker means to say draw.
